reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Parasomnias are undesirable physical or experiential events that intrude on sleep and are broadly divided by the sleep stage from which they arise into non-REM (NREM) and REM types

NREM disorders of arousal (confusional arousals, sleepwalking, night terrors) typically occur in the first third of the night during deep slow-wave sleep, with the person appearing awake but confused and having little or no recall
REM sleep behaviour disorder involves loss of the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep, so patients physically act out vivid, often violent dreams and can injure themselves or a bed partner
REM sleep behaviour disorder is strongly associated with, and may precede by years, neurodegenerative alpha-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies
NREM parasomnias are common and usually benign in children, tending to resolve with age, whereas new-onset events in adults warrant more careful evaluation
Triggers that deepen or fragment sleep, including sleep deprivation, alcohol, fever, stress, and certain medications, can precipitate NREM events
Management prioritises sleep hygiene, safety-proofing the bedroom, and removal of precipitants; pharmacological treatment is reserved for frequent, dangerous, or distressing episodes
Nocturnal frontal-lobe seizures can mimic parasomnias and should be considered when events are stereotyped, very frequent, or occur repeatedly within a single night
reference.pathophysiology: Parasomnias reflect incomplete or dysregulated transitions between wakefulness and sleep states rather than a single disease. In NREM disorders of arousal, partial awakening from slow-wave sleep leaves motor and autonomic systems active while consciousness and memory circuits remain asleep, producing complex behaviours without awareness; a genetic predisposition and any factor that increases slow-wave sleep or arousal frequency raises the risk. REM sleep behaviour disorder results from failure of the brainstem circuits that normally impose skeletal muscle atonia during REM sleep, allowing dream enactment; the underlying neuronal dysfunction is closely linked to synucleinopathy neurodegeneration. Other parasomnias, such as sleep-related eating or nightmare disorder, arise from analogous state-boundary instability.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive sleep apnoea with confusional arousals
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history from patient and bed partner, including timing within the night and degree of recall
Video polysomnography with expanded EEG montage to capture events and exclude seizures
Neurological assessment and, where indicated, dopaminergic imaging when REM sleep behaviour disorder is suspected
Screening for coexisting sleep apnoea as a trigger for arousals
Review of medications and substances that can provoke parasomnias
redFlags: Dream enactment with violent behaviour suggesting REM sleep behaviour disorder and possible underlying neurodegeneration
New-onset complex nocturnal behaviour in an adult without childhood history
Stereotyped, repetitive episodes clustering within one night raising suspicion of nocturnal seizures
Episodes causing injury to the patient or bed partner
reference.prognosis: Most childhood NREM parasomnias are benign and remit spontaneously; adult NREM events can often be controlled by addressing precipitants, while REM sleep behaviour disorder tends to persist and carries an appreciable long-term risk of evolving neurodegenerative disease.
pitfalls: Mislabelling nocturnal seizures as benign parasomnia and delaying appropriate neurological workup
Failing to counsel patients with REM sleep behaviour disorder about future neurodegenerative risk and bedroom safety
Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as the arousal trigger driving NREM events
Attempting to forcibly wake a sleepwalker, which may increase agitation and injury risk
